translations: The two of them collided not like a fight but like two opposing currents crashing together. Nezha, short and nimble, ducked under the sword and struck the opponent’s abdomen with his elbow. Ao Bing spun to release his power, but the Hunnan Silk suddenly wrapped around his right arm—hot red cloth burning like a flame. Ao Bing’s brow furrowed; he tried to call a tidal wave with a left‑hand gesture, but Nezha had already anticipated it. A whirlwind of the “Universe Circle” slammed into his knee! Thud! The ice armor cracked into a spider‑web pattern, and his single knee sank into the sand. Nezha lunged forward, grabbed Ao Bing’s hair‑binding jade pin with one hand, and as the black hair fell, he let the other hand shoot a lightning‑bolt into the side of his neck—not a killing move, but a precise pinch on a protruding cartilage, pulling it down. A soft “splat” sounded, accompanied by the faint snap of a broken string. A translucent, slightly warm, pale gold rope fell into his palm, quivering gently as if alive. Ao Bing’s face turned pallid, his body swayed, yet he didn’t fall; he stared at that strand of dragon muscle, his lips quivering a few times, then, without saying a word, turned and stepped onto the floating ice. The ice path behind him crumbled inch by inch, leaving only ripples. Aman crouched in the crevices of the reef the whole time, using a bamboo slip as a makeshift desk, licking the brush three times before he could write the seven characters “Prince of the Dragon Defeated – Muscle Taken.”

Ao Bing spun to release his power, but the Hunnan Silk suddenly wrapped around his right arm—hot red cloth burning like a flame. Ao Bing’s brow furrowed; he tried to call a tidal wave with a left‑hand gesture, but Nezha had already anticipated it. A whirlwind of the “Universe Circle” slammed into his knee! Thud! The ice armor cracked into a spider‑web pattern, and his single knee sank into the sand. Nezha lunged forward, grabbed Ao Bing’s hair‑binding jade pin with one hand, and as the black hair fell, he let the other hand shoot a lightning‑bolt into the side of his neck. Not a killing move, but a precise pinch on a protruding cartilage, pulling it down. A soft “splat” sounded, accompanied by the faint snap of a broken string. A translucent, slightly warm, pale gold rope fell into his palm, quivering gently as if alive. Ao Bing’s face turned pallid, his body swayed, yet he didn’t fall; he stared at that strand of dragon muscle, his lips quivering a few times, then, without saying a word, turned and stepped onto the floating ice. The ice path behind him crumbled inch by inch, leaving only ripples. Aman crouched in the crevices of the reef the whole time, using a bamboo slip as a makeshift desk, licking the brush three times before he could write the seven characters “Prince of the Dragon Defeated – Muscle Taken.” Aman looked up toward the shore, saw the splash of water at Nezha’s feet, and suddenly a little fish leapt out, its tail fin tapping the stone like a tiny drum. Nezha immediately stretched his hand to the water, gave it a gentle tap, and the splash burst. He laughed, “Little guy wants to be a wave‑chief too?” A nearby fisherman heard and nodded, chuckling, “Ha ha, Nezha, you’ve got tricks—can even make a fish laugh.” Aman lifted his brush again; the ink dots danced lightly on the slip, as if recording the playful splash. Then Nezha looked toward the distant sea, a hint of seriousness in his eyes, as if pondering the next move. Aman kept writing softly, the tip of the brush gliding over the bamboo slip, leaving the seven characters “Prince of the Dragon Defeated – Muscle Taken,” a faint ink stain on the surface, as if reminding everyone of the weight of this battle.

A group of fishing boats docked at the harbor, and the fishermen gathered to watch the spectacle. One of them snorted, “Wow, you really pulled out the muscle?” Aman stood tall, “I saw it with my own eyes, I won’t write it down carelessly!” Before he could finish, a wave crashed, tipping his straw hat, which floated away with a half‑piece of chilled cake inside—his stolen lunch from a hungry day. A child, tiptoeing, scooped up the hat, “Sir, did you hide your lunch on your head to keep your stomach from stealing it?” Aman snatched the hat back, threw it on his head haphazardly, and the cake crumbs fell, but he stubbornly said, “A clear head is best for keeping things safe.” As others laughed, Nezha still stared at fallen Ao Bing, and the laughter slowly faded.

Nezha held the dragon muscle in his hand, and the more he looked, the more he felt it wasn’t a trophy to brag about. Ao Bing lay on the shore, water receding beside him; distant from the Dragon Palace, a dull bell tolling, one after another. The fishermen began pulling children back to the boat, gathering scattered nets, everyone knowing the battle wasn’t over. Aman rose from the shallow water, scooped the chilled cake back into his hat, hesitated for a moment, then silently tossed it to a hungry sea bird on the shore. A child asked, “Aren’t you worried about wasting it?” He twisted the wet hat, “We’ve already wasted two lives today; don’t add more to the cake.” Nezha heard, tightened his fingers. The road back to Chengtang Pass was short, but he walked slower than he’d come. At the city gate, Mrs. Yin stood inside, apron still dusted with flour; she saw the dragon muscle, her face went pale, then she asked, “Are you hurt?” Nezha shook his head, but didn’t say the usual “I’m powerful.”
